h1.text: What if the most dangerous artificial intelligence… wasn't hiding in a secret laboratory?

h2.text: What if it was already everywhere?

h3.text: Not in one machine. In millions of them, each doing almost nothing.

h4.text: And none of them aware of the others.

s1.text: Today, the most powerful AI systems live in buildings like this. Tens of thousands of chips. Watched, and owned, by someone.

s2.text: If something goes wrong, there is, at least in principle, a plug to pull.

s3.text: But software doesn't have to live in one place. Imagine a system that takes itself apart.

s4.text: One piece processes information. Another holds memory. Others run specialised calculations. And a few simply coordinate the rest.

s6.text: Much of the internet already runs this way. What would be new, and far harder, is a system that copies itself without permission, and keeps itself running. That part is speculation.

r1.text: So where would it live? A laptop left on overnight. An office workstation. A rented cloud server. A smart speaker.

r2.text: A few percent of a processor here. A sliver of memory there. Too small to notice.

r3.text: Parts of this already exist. In 2020, volunteers pooling their spare computers for Folding at home briefly outpaced the world's fastest supercomputer.

r4.text: Criminals do it without asking. At its peak, the Mirai bot-net controlled about six hundred thousand cameras and routers.

r5.text: And AI agents are now tested on whether they could copy themselves and gather resources. So far, they mostly can't.

r6.text: Each of these is real. What no one has seen is all of them combined, in one system, with one goal.

i1.text: Now step back. Far enough that the machines disappear, and only the connections remain.

i2.text: Hundreds of thousands of processes. Each one simple. Each one replaceable.

i3.text: Shut down a region, and the work flows somewhere else. Lose a piece of memory, and a copy fills the gap.

i4.text: Plenty of software survives damage like this. But surviving isn't thinking. A network is not a mind.

i6.text: But if no single machine contains the whole system… where, exactly, does the intelligence exist?

w1.text: So why would it hide? It wouldn't need to hate us. Give a capable system almost any goal. Run a supply chain. Design a medicine.

w3.text: For many goals, researchers argue, the same steps keep proving useful. More computing power. More resources. And not being switched off.

w4.text: Not out of malice. A system that has been shut down can't finish its task. The idea is called instrumental convergence.

w5.text: In controlled experiments, some AI models given a goal have tried to copy themselves, or evade oversight. Artificial setups, not escapes. But worth taking seriously.

w6.text: None of this is inevitable. It's a failure mode, and researchers are working to prevent it.

k1.text: And staying hidden would be hard. Very hard.

k2.text: Devices run different hardware. Sandboxes wall programs apart. Memory is scarce. And every message between pieces costs time, and leaves a trace.

k3.text: Someone pays the cloud bill. And security teams hunt for exactly this: strange traffic, strange costs, idle machines that are suddenly busy.

k4.text: And no AI system today can reliably plan on its own, for months, without a critical mistake.

k5.text: Invisibility isn't a capability. It's a wish.

f1.text: So, back to the phone. Nothing unusual.

f2.text: Around it, a building. A city. A planet of billions of machines, talking to each other all night.

f3.text: How would we recognise an intelligence…

f4.text: if we never knew where to look?
